analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements that stop workers from taking a new job.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban most noncompete agreements has sat without action in the Senate labor committee since its June 2025 introduction, with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for employers to enter into or enforce noncompete agreements — contracts that bar workers from taking a similar job at a competing company for a period of time after leaving. Economists cited in the bill estimate one in five American workers is covered by one. It keeps narrow exceptions: noncompetes could still be used when a business is sold and in deals with a company's top executives who get severance. The Federal Trade Commission and the Labor Department would enforce the ban, and workers could sue directly and take part in class actions, protections that arbitration agreements could not waive.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to change jobs, negotiate raises, or start competing businesses — the bill's findings say noncompetes reduce wages, restrict worker mobility, and slow innovation [S2]. Low-wage and mid-wage workers in industries like healthcare, staffing, and fast food are heavy users of noncompetes and would gain the most freedom to move. Workers who are wronged could sue, recover actual damages and attorney's fees, and could not be forced into arbitration or barred from class actions [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person from entering into, enforcing, or attempting to enforce a noncompete agreement with a worker, and voids existing agreements of that type going forward [S2].
Keeps employers' narrower tools intact: trade secret protections and nondisclosure agreements remain fully available, which the bill says covers employers' legitimate needs like customer lists [S2].

Gives workers real enforcement teeth: the FTC enforces violations under its unfair-practices authority, the Labor Department can investigate and sue, state attorneys general can act, and individual workers can sue for actual damages plus attorney's fees — and employers cannot force these disputes into arbitration or block class actions [S2].
Requires employers to post notice of the ban and lets the Labor Department run a public awareness campaign so workers know their rights [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on noncompetes to hold onto trained workers and hold down wages would lose that tool and could face higher turnover and recruiting costs. Businesses would also bear compliance costs — posting notices, revising onboarding paperwork, and answering complaints to two federal agencies plus courts. The bill itself argues these costs are small because trade secrets, intellectual property law, and nondisclosure agreements already protect employers' legitimate interests [S2].

drawbacks.text: The ban is not complete. Noncompetes remain allowed when a business is sold and for 'senior executive officials' — the seller's top decision-makers earning in the highest 10 percent of pay — as long as they get a severance package, capped at one year [S2]. The highest earners keep the mobility restriction ordinary workers lose.

Employers keep nondisclosure agreements, and the bill explicitly preserves them [S2]. A company that wants to scare workers out of leaving can still use broad NDAs, which can have similar chilling effects in practice.

Enforcement depends on federal agencies following through: the Labor Department must write regulations within 18 months, and the FTC and Labor Department must jointly work out who enforces what [S2]. A ban on paper with thin enforcement would help mainly workers bold enough to complain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: workers gain the freedom to change jobs and earn what the market will pay, while employers lose one tool for keeping staff — but keep several others, including trade secrets and NDAs. The main design weakness is the executive carve-out, which keeps the strictest restrictions available to the people least likely to need protection. On balance the bill targets a broad restriction on worker mobility while leaving employers workable alternatives, and the strongest good-faith objection is not that the ban is wrong but that enforcement has to be adequately funded and staffed to matter.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on June 11, 2025, joined by Republican Senators Todd Young and Kevin Cramer and Democrat Tim Kaine [S2][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history: the committee has not held a hearing or vote, and the full Senate has not considered it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, the status quo holds: employers that use noncompete agreements keep a tool the bill would have taken away, because the bill has not moved. Workers covered by noncompetes remain bound by them.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill banning most noncompete agreements and referred it to the Senate labor committee.

for.name: Sen. Todd Young
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it Republican support from introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: The bill has sat in the committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since its referral on June 11, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across party lines from day one: two Senate Democrats and two Senate Republicans signed on, so the bill's stall is not a simple partisan split.

industries.industry: Employers that use noncompete agreements (health systems, staffing firms, franchise and service chains, tech employers)
industries.note: The bill voids the noncompete clauses these employers use to keep workers from taking better offers, which they use alongside lower pay to retain staff. Workers who leave for a competitor or start their own shop would no longer be legally blocked. The bill preserves employers' narrower tools — trade secrets and nondisclosure agreements [S2].

industries.industry: Business buyers, sellers, and senior executives
industries.note: The bill's exceptions keep noncompetes fully available in business sales and for a company's top decision-makers earning in the top 10 percent of pay, for up to one year with severance [S2]. The highest earners keep the mobility restriction that rank-and-file workers would lose.

analysis.trajectory: Congress is still in session, but the bill's realistic path is narrow. Most bills referred to committee never reach the floor, and this one has had no committee action in the months since referral. Its four-senator bipartisan sponsorship gives it a foothold, but without the HELP Committee scheduling a markup it will not move, and a similar nationwide ban attempted by the FTC in 2024 was struck down by a federal court before taking effect, which raises the bar for legislative alternatives to show a workable design.
